messages.content: Write a post about what a software company learned from a year of remote work. Around 250 words.

output:
A year into remote work, most of what we thought we knew turned out wrong.

We started by copying the office onto video calls: daily standups, back-to-back meetings, a chat channel for every team. Attendance stayed high. Output dropped. People were logging in and saying less. It took a few months to notice that the problem wasn't remote work itself — it was that we'd kept the meeting culture and lost the hallway conversations that used to make those meetings short.

The fix wasn't a new tool. We cut recurring meetings by half and asked every team to write a short daily update instead: what shipped, what's blocked, what's next. Engineers read them when it suited their schedule, not on someone else's clock. Two quarters later, cycle time on tickets was down 18%, and nobody missed the meetings we'd cut.

We also learned that time zones aren't a problem to route around — they're a scheduling constraint like any other. Once we assigned each project a home time zone and let async updates carry the rest, cross-team handoffs stopped losing a day to waiting on a reply.

The clearest lesson: presence isn't proof of work, and a packed calendar isn't proof of collaboration. What moved the numbers was writing things down, trusting people to read them, and freeing up the hours that used to go to meetings nobody wanted.

We're still adjusting. But a year in, the team ships faster with fewer meetings than it did in the office.
